questions.q: What does a reflection step add to an agent's process, per this lesson?
options: It forces the agent to repeat the exact same output twice for redundancy
It disables tool use for the remainder of the session
It has the agent (or a second pass) critique its own intermediate output or plan and revise it, catching mistakes earlier stages missed
It replaces the need for any human review permanently
questions.explain: Reflection evaluates a draft answer or plan against the goal, often catching logical errors or missed details before they propagate further.

questions.q: What does Anthropic call the generate/evaluate/revise loop, and how are the two roles structured?
options: The 'single-pass' workflow — generation and evaluation always happen in one combined step
The evaluator-optimizer workflow — one call generates a response while a separate call evaluates it and provides feedback, looping until satisfied
The 'retry-forever' workflow — there is no evaluation step, only blind repetition
The 'human-only' workflow — evaluation can never be performed by a model
questions.explain: Generation and evaluation are deliberately treated as different roles, even when the same underlying model plays both, which is what lets mistakes get caught rather than compounding unchecked.

questions.q: In the contract termination clause example, what kind of mistake did reflection catch?
options: A tool-calling error where the wrong function was invoked
A formatting error in the JSON response
A plausible-sounding, confidently wrong summary that omitted the actual notice period and early-termination fee from the source clause
A network timeout error from a third-party API
questions.explain: The first draft read fine on its own but didn't match the real source clause — exactly the kind of error a single generate-and-stop pass would ship without ever checking it.

questions.q: Does reflection replace patterns like ReAct, planning, or orchestrator/worker from earlier in this chapter?
options: Yes, reflection makes all of those patterns obsolete and unnecessary
Yes, reflection can only be used completely on its own, never combined with anything
No, reflection can only ever be applied to ReAct specifically
No — reflection is an additional layer that can wrap around any of them, such as a planning agent reflecting on its plan before executing
questions.explain: Reflection is a layer added on top of the earlier-stage pattern being used, not a competing alternative to it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of output is reflection's cost specifically worth paying for?
options: Outputs where a wrong-but-confident answer is worse than the extra round trip, such as summaries of source material or generated code that will be acted on without independent re-checking
Every single output an agent ever produces, with no exceptions
Outputs that never involve any language generation at all
Only outputs that cost nothing in tokens to produce
questions.explain: Like every pattern in this chapter, reflection adds a real cost (another model call, more latency); it earns that cost on high-stakes outputs, not universally.
